stemMd: Which of the following best describes the function of the final paragraph?

options.label: A
options.textMd: It concludes that simplification makes every model, physical or numerical, unreliable.

options.label: B
options.textMd: It extends a principle learned from physical models to the computer models that followed.

options.label: C
options.textMd: It calls for physical models to be rebuilt so that computer results can be checked.

options.label: D
options.textMd: It explains that the halls were emptied because physical models gave wrong answers.

options.label: E
options.textMd: It argues that computer models are less trustworthy than the physical models they replaced.

explanationMd:
Read the final paragraph for its turning word. It opens with a fact (the halls have been emptied) and then turns: "Yet the discipline they taught survived the move to the computer." The word "also", repeated three times, ties numerical models to physical ones: both simplify, both are tuned, and both are trusted only if they "can first reproduce what the river is known to have done", the very test the third paragraph described. "The concrete has gone; the test remains" sums it up. The paragraph carries a principle from the old models over to the new ones.

Check the rivals. The reason given for emptying the halls is cost and speed, not wrong answers. The repeated "also" puts the two kinds of model on the same footing, so the paragraph does not rank one above the other, and it asks for no halls to be rebuilt. Nor does it say every simplified model is unreliable: it says such a model deserves trust once it passes the test.

distractorRationale.e: The paragraph uses "also" three times to put numerical models under the same conditions as physical ones. It does not rank them, and says a numerical model deserves trust when it passes the test.
distractorRationale.d: The reason given is that numerical models "became cheaper and quicker to run". Physical models giving wrong answers is a problem the second paragraph says was overcome by distortion, not the reason they were abandoned.
distractorRationale.c: The paragraph says the test survives inside the computer: numerical models are checked by reproducing what the river has done. It never asks for physical models to be rebuilt.
distractorRationale.a: The paragraph says a model "deserves trust" to the extent that it reproduces known behaviour. Simplification is a condition to check, not a reason to dismiss every model.

accessibilityText: A purpose question about the river models passage. It asks which statement best describes the function of the final paragraph. The five choices: It concludes that simplification makes every model, physical or numerical, unreliable; It extends a principle learned from physical models to the computer models that followed; It calls for physical models to be rebuilt so that computer results can be checked; It explains that the halls were emptied because physical models gave wrong answers; It argues that computer models are less trustworthy than the physical models they replaced.

provenance.notes: Original item written for this bank against an original passage; it tests the function of a concluding paragraph that generalises the passage's method. Every option is answerable, or refutable, from the passage text alone.

independentSolve.workingNotes: The final paragraph says 'the discipline they taught survived the move to the computer': numerical models must also first reproduce known behaviour. So it extends a principle from physical models to computer models. It does not call every model unreliable (trust is conditional) or ask for the halls to be rebuilt. It says the halls emptied because numerical models were cheaper and quicker, not because physical models were wrong, and it does not rank computer models below physical ones. [A second, separate blind solve (blind-reviewer-wave8-tolci-verbal-run1) reached the same answer: The final paragraph says the discipline of physical models (trust only after reproducing known behaviour) survived in numerical models: extending a principle. Halls were emptied because computers were cheaper/quicker, not because physical models were wrong; no call to rebuild them, no claim that all models are unreliable or that computer models are less trustworthy.]
